# Preface {.unnumbered}

This report documents the applications shipped with OpenPFC 0.2: what each one
solves, how it is discretised, how it is verified, and — where it has been
measured — how it scales.

Every chapter follows the same shape, and it starts with the physics rather
than the mathematics. First the **physical question**: what object is being
simulated, and which observable answers the question being asked of it. Then a
**Problem setup** table giving the domain, grid, boundary conditions, initial
condition, parameters and observable of the configuration actually shipped,
followed by a sentence on what the idealisations — periodicity above all —
mean physically for that particular problem and what they leave out. Only then
come the governing equations, in the form a physicist would write them, and the
discrete formulation: for the spectral applications the reciprocal-space
symbol, and for the finite-difference applications the stencil and update rule.
Each chapter then states what is actually verified in the test suite, so a
claim in this report can be traced to an assertion in the repository.

Two conventions in those tables are worth explaining once.

**Verification presets are labelled as such.** Several applications ship a
small configuration whose answer is known in closed form alongside a larger one
that is meant to represent something physical. These are not interchangeable,
and a verification preset is never presented here as a production science case.

**Model maturity is reported on three independent axes**, never collapsed into
a single word, because a model can be excellent on one and absent on another:

* *numerical verification* — analytical, manufactured, regression, or none;
* *physical completeness* — canonical, reduced, or extended;
* *calibration* — none, representative, or quantitative.

An application with an exact closed-form check and entirely made-up parameters
is analytically verified and uncalibrated, and saying so is more useful than
calling it either "verified" or "uncalibrated" on its own.

The report is written in Quarto. It has no compute engine: the scalability
figures are committed SVGs regenerated by `figures/make_figures.py` from the
CSV files under `data/`, which are themselves transcribed from
[`docs/hpc/lumi_gpu_scaling.md`](../hpc/lumi_gpu_scaling.md).

```bash
quarto render docs/report          # HTML
quarto render docs/report --to pdf # PDF
```

::: {.callout-note}
## Status

This is a first draft. Every shipped application now carries a physical
question, a problem-setup table and a three-axis maturity statement, and the
mathematics and verification sections are complete. Sixteen applications are
in the catalog; the sixteenth (`inverse_homogenization`) is an explicit
exception for PDE-constrained inverse design, not a licence to grow the set. The scalability chapter covers the two models (tungsten and
Heat3D) that have been measured on LUMI-G out to 16 nodes; Vlasov scaling is
in its own chapter and stops at the $N_{v_y}$ rank cap. The remaining
applications are marked as unmeasured rather than estimated. Where a parameter
could not be traced to a source from this repository, the chapter says so
instead of implying a provenance it does not have.
:::
